newsReadings.title: Cooling the Planet on Purpose: The Geoengineering Debate Ahead of COP31
newsReadings.source: The Times, 'Climate scientists want billions to study cooling the planet,' 3 November 2026
newsReadings.passage:
As delegates prepare to travel to Turkey for COP31, the United Nations climate conference opening on 9 November, a striking proposal has entered the debate: that Britain and other nations should together spend tens of billions of pounds a year investigating ways to cool the planet deliberately. The call comes from a group led by Sir David King, the government's former chief scientific adviser, and reflects a growing anxiety that cutting emissions alone may no longer be sufficient to prevent dangerous warming.

The techniques under discussion, collectively known as geoengineering, range from the familiar to the futuristic. One approach, marine cloud brightening, would spray fine seawater droplets or deliver an electric current from drones to make clouds more reflective, bouncing more sunlight back into space. Another would inject tiny particles into the stratosphere, mimicking the natural cooling that follows a large volcanic eruption. More radical ideas include pumping seawater onto Arctic ice so that it freezes and thickens, artificially encouraging the plankton blooms that absorb carbon dioxide, and using machines to suck greenhouse gases directly from the air and store them underground. A Swiss company, Climeworks, already operates such machines in Iceland, while an American-Israeli start-up, Project Stardust, has raised 75 million dollars to inject particles into the atmosphere.

Britain, according to King, is already ahead of most countries in this research. The government is spending 67 million pounds exploring ways to address global warming, with about 10.5 million pounds channelled through UK Research and Innovation and the remainder through the Advanced Research and Invention Agency, the so-called moonshot research programme. King's Climate Crisis Advisory Group argues, however, that this remains far too little. It calls on countries including Australia, France and Japan to contribute collectively to spending of about 22.2 billion pounds a year — a figure that underlines how seriously its authors regard the threat after a summer of widespread heatwaves and drought.

Crucially, the report insists that researching geoengineering is not a licence to deploy it. Britain has made clear that although it funds research, it does not support deployment, and the report itself warns that technologies must be investigated before any decision about their use could responsibly be taken. That distinction matters because the risks are substantial. The Royal Society has warned that injudicious use of such technology could worsen extreme weather in some parts of the world, shifting rainfall patterns or disrupting monsoons on which hundreds of millions depend. A technology that cools the planet on average could still harm particular regions, raising profound questions about who decides, who benefits and who bears the cost.

Supporters argue that the alternative — refusing even to study these options — is itself a gamble. If emissions cuts continue to fall short and temperatures overshoot agreed limits, societies may one day face a choice between untested interventions and catastrophic climate impacts, with no evidence base on which to decide. Research now, on this view, preserves future options without committing anyone to using them. Public opinion appears broadly sympathetic to investigation: polling of 15,000 adults in Britain and the United States, conducted by Dynata and commissioned by the Climate Crisis Advisory Group, found that 78 per cent support more geoengineering research.

Critics counter that the promise of a technological fix could undermine the urgency of cutting emissions, offering polluters an excuse to delay. They also note that some techniques, such as stratospheric particle injection, would need to be maintained indefinitely; stopping abruptly could cause temperatures to rebound rapidly. Governance, they argue, remains unresolved: there is no international body with clear authority to approve planetary-scale experiments, let alone deployment. As COP31 approaches, therefore, the debate is less about whether any single technique works than about how humanity should govern knowledge that could reshape the climate itself. The scientists' message is deliberately narrow: study the options seriously, in the open, before desperation forces a decision in the dark.

questions.q: Why does the Climate Crisis Advisory Group call for much larger geoengineering research spending?
options: Because deployment has already been approved.
Because it fears emissions cuts alone may not prevent dangerous warming.
Because Britain has no research programme.

questions.q: What is marine cloud brightening intended to do?
options: Make clouds more reflective so more sunlight bounces back into space.
Remove all clouds from the sky.

questions.q: How much is Britain already spending on this research, according to the passage?
What warning does the Royal Society give?
options: That research should be banned immediately.
That injudicious use could worsen extreme weather in some regions.

questions.q: What concern do critics raise about stratospheric particle injection?
options: It would need to be maintained indefinitely, and stopping could cause rapid rebound warming.
It would cool the planet too quickly in all regions.
It has already been deployed worldwide.

questions.q: The passage states that Britain funds geoengineering research but does not support deployment.
The passage states that 78 per cent of those polled opposed more geoengineering research.

newsReadings.title: Walking, Grasping, Repeating: A Humanoid Robot Learns to Chain Tasks
newsReadings.source: Tech Xplore, 'Humanoid AI connects walking and object handling without demonstrations of complete task sequences,' 2 November 2026
newsReadings.passage:
Ask a humanoid robot to walk across a room, pick up a bottle and place it on a table, and you are asking it to solve a surprisingly difficult problem. Walking and grasping involve different joints, different rhythms and different kinds of control. A robot that walks well may fumble when it reaches for an object, while one trained to manipulate objects may stumble when it tries to move. Until recently, teaching a robot to perform such multistage tasks required demonstrations of the entire sequence, filmed and recorded from start to finish — a laborious process in which a failure at any intermediate stage could render the whole demonstration useless.

A team led by Professor Songhwai Oh at Seoul National University has now proposed a more economical solution. Their framework, called RISE — Responsibility-Induced Specialized Experts — is a vision-language-action model that learns jointly from locomotion and object-manipulation data collected separately. In other words, the robot is shown examples of walking on its own, and examples of picking up and placing objects on their own, but never a complete demonstration of walking, picking up and placing in sequence. The system must learn, by itself, when one behaviour should end and the next should begin.

RISE achieves this through a distinctive architecture. A shared visual-language perception model interprets camera images and natural-language instructions such as pick up the object and move it to the designated location. Beneath it sit multiple action experts, coordinated by a meta-controller. During training, the system evaluates how accurately each expert predicts the current action and calculates its responsibility: experts with higher responsibility exert greater influence when learning from the corresponding data. Without any predefined roles, individual experts therefore specialise naturally, some becoming adept at locomotion and others at manipulation. During execution, changes in the weights assigned by the meta-controller serve as signals for transitions, allowing the robot to recognise that its current task has finished and to move smoothly to the next one.

The results, validated both in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid robot, are striking. In simulation, robots performed two- to four-stage tasks involving apples, bottles and cups, such as moving and then picking up an object, or moving, picking up, moving again and placing the object down. RISE achieved an average success rate of 87.3 per cent, outperforming the 73.6 per cent of a baseline built on NVIDIA's GR00T foundation model with a single-expert architecture. On the real robot — equipped with two Dex3-1 robotic hands in addition to its whole-body joints, giving 43 controllable degrees of freedom — RISE completed two-, four- and up to five-stage tasks with an average success rate of 50.0 per cent, twenty percentage points higher than the baseline's 30.0 per cent. Importantly, its advantage grew as tasks became longer, precisely where transitions matter most.

The significance of the work lies less in any single demonstration than in what it implies for how humanoid robots are trained. Collecting complete, continuous demonstrations for every conceivable task is prohibitively expensive and fragile. If robots can instead learn from separately collected behaviours and combine them autonomously, training becomes far more scalable. The same responsibility-based approach could eventually integrate other behaviours with different characteristics, including bimanual manipulation and tool use, within a single system. The research was accepted for the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026).

Practical applications are already visible on the horizon. Humanoids capable of alternating locomotion and manipulation could transport goods in logistics centres, move parts and tools in manufacturing environments, and, as safety and adaptability improve, carry supplies in hospitals, assist with caregiving and organise objects in homes. Professor Oh cautions that the current system still performs behaviours sequentially, and the team's next ambition is more demanding still: manipulating objects while moving, a whole-body coordination that humans perform effortlessly but robots find exceptionally hard. For now, RISE demonstrates a crucial step — that a robot need not be shown an entire task to learn how to perform it, provided its experts know, collectively, when to hand over.

questions.q: Why is teaching multistage tasks traditionally difficult?
options: Because robots cannot walk at all.
Because a failure at any stage can render a complete demonstration useless.
Because cameras do not work indoors.

questions.q: What data does RISE learn from?
options: Complete demonstrations of every task sequence.
Locomotion and manipulation data collected separately.

questions.q: How do experts in RISE specialise?
options: They are assigned fixed roles by programmers.
Through responsibility scores based on prediction accuracy, without predefined roles.
By copying the GR00T model exactly.
RISE 87.3 per cent versus a GR00T-based baseline of 73.6 per cent.
RISE 50.0 per cent versus 30.0 per cent.
RISE scored lower than the baseline.

questions.q: What is the team's next ambition, according to Professor Oh?
options: To move beyond sequential behaviour to manipulating objects while moving.
To build a robot with no hands.

questions.q: The passage states that the real Unitree G1 robot had 43 controllable degrees of freedom.
The passage states that RISE was shown complete demonstrations of walking, picking up and placing in sequence.
